utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. For the next witness to be called, there was an application for protective measures: Pseudonym, face distortion, and voice distortion. There were no objections against it. The Chamber grants the protective measures. The standard the Chamber uses is that there should be an objectively grounded risk to the security or the welfare of the witness or the witness's family. It shouldn't become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal, and this standard can be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family, or a combination of the following, and that would apply in this case: That the witness testimony may antagonise persons who reside in the specific territory; that the witness or his or her family live or work in that territory, have property in that territory, or have concrete plans to return to live in the territory; and that there exists an unstable security situation in that territory, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. Less, the last part to have test, the parties agreed that this condition is fulfilled in Kosovo. So, therefore, on the second grounds, the combination of the three elements, the Chamber grants the protective measures. The witness will testify under pseudonym 68. The witness will testify with face and voice distortion. The parties are invited to switch off their microphones when the witness answers questions. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. There is one -- one other matter, and that's for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- witness coming after this, the next witness. With regard to the, I believe it's some, 90 annexes that have been attached to -- I believe he's not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness is not protected, as far as I know, and that's Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic. With regard to the annexes that have been attached to Mr. Zivanovic's statements, of which I believe there are 90, 25 of them do not appear on the 65 ter list. No application has been made. No good cause has been shown why there has been this addition or why this addition is necessary, and we object to their admission at this time. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- specify either right now on the record or shortly send a filing in, so that you have the specific annex numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it would be better not to read it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be a burden for translators, transcribers. Mr. Di Fazio, I don't know who is dealing with the witness next to come. MR. DI FAZIO: My colleague, Ms. Gustafson is taking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Gustafson, could you explain why 25 exhibits are used that are not on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's some confusion. The witness after this next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- is being taken by Mr. Re, and we'll communicate the message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll communicate the objections. MR. DI FAZIO: I apologise. I misunderstood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I wasn't clear, as a matter of fact. Yes. I said, "the witness next to come," which is not very clear language. I apologise for that. Then, Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom and the curtains down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, perhaps I'll already indicate the following -- no, I'll wait until we are there. Is there any summary of the 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was sent to the Defence last night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- and I think to the Chamber this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not looked at my e-mail this morning, but I'll do it immediately. Yes. If it has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted), before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning again. The Chamber has decided that we will not use your name. We will call you Witness 68, and your face will not be seen by those outside this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your own voice will not be heard by those outside this courtroom; however, the content of your testimony is available to the public. Ms. Gustafson, who's counsel for the Prosecution, will now examine you. Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for granting my wish not to have my name mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, could you switch off your microphone whenever the witness speaks. But now you can switch it on again, because it's you who will speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 2082, to be -- to be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P1015, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 68, could you please look at the screen and just please confirm with a "yes" or a "no" whether those personal details are correct and whether the person described in that sheet is you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: On that basis, could we admit the pseudonym sheet into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, it's admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 2080, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P1016, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we please go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 68, do you recognise this document as a statement that you signed on the 9th of October, 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is that statement that you made true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I asked you in court today the same questions that you were asked when you gave that statement, would you give the Court the same answers that are in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've prepared a redacted version of this statement with paragraph 17 through 19 redacted. Could that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Then it's admitted into evidence, the redacted version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At this time, I propose to read a brief summary of the witness's statement onto the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so, that is not P1016, because P1016 was the full version, so therefore I take it that the redacted version -- or are you tendering both?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the redacted version, and that's P1016?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It was 65 ter number 2080.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The one that the witness just saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then that's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In 1998, Witness 68 lived in the town of Pec with her husband and their three children. Witness 68 is Serbian. Witness 68 saw her husband for the last time on the morning of 16 July 1998, when he was leaving for work. He worked as a market inspector for the municipality of Pec. Witness 68's husband told Witness 68 that before going to work he would visit some relatives in Djakovica and then see some relatives in the village of Dobric on his way home. He wanted to see how his relatives in Dobric were doing, because they had been attacked by the KLA a few days earlier. At around 1330 hours that day, Witness 68's husband called her to tell her that he was leaving Djakovica for the village of Dobric. That was the last time Witness 68 heard from her husband. At approximately 2100 hours that evening, Witness 68 called the SUP in Pec. The Pec SUP told Witness 68 that they had heard from their colleagues at the Djakovica SUP that Witness 68's husband had been kidnapped by KLA members in the village of Dujak. In September 1998, Witness 68 was told by the Djakovica MUP that they had arrested a group of KLA members and that two of the arrested KLA members, Ljuan and Krist Perforci from Dujak, had kidnapped Witness 68's husband. Witness 68 left Kosovo with her three children on 14 June 1999, together with the withdrawing VJ and MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 68, your statement has been admitted as evidence, so I'm only going to ask you a few questions, and these questions will all relate to what you learned after your husband disappeared about what had happened to him. You've said in your statement that in September 1998, you got a call from the MUP in Djakovica telling you that they had arrested a group of KLA members responsible for your husband's kidnapping, and you've also said that you went to the Djakovica MUP, where the MUP told you that two individuals with the last name of Perforci had kidnapped your husband. Now, my first question is: When was it that you went to the Djakovica MUP? Was it the same day that they had called you or was it a later day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: When I went for identification, that was the day I went there; however, they didn't know anything. Several days later they called me again and told me that there was a group of people who had attacked the MUP building there, that they had arrested some, and that they believed that among them were people who had kidnapped my husband. I believe it was in late September.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how long after they called you did you actually go to the MUP building in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: I believe, I believe it was on the following day that I went there or two or three days later. I can't recall exactly. The first time I went to SUP, they weren't able to tell me anything, and I believe that I -- the next time I went there was right after they called me, and it was two or three days after the first visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you went to the MUP in Djakovica on this occasion, after they had telephoned you about the arrests, it was then that the MUP told you about these two individuals by the name of Perforci who had been responsible for your husband's kidnapping; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did the MUP officials tell you how they had learned that it was these two individuals by the name of Perforci who had kidnapped your husband?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, forgive me. We're obviously entering territory now which raises the issue of this witness potentially having seen documents. The documents themselves do not appear on the face of the material we have to be available, and there is an objection, as Your Honours know, to both the documents which are available and to the tendering through a witness of her recollection of documents which are not available. And, so, at this stage, I wish to place on the record our objection to this aspect of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- all counsel share this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the objection is there. We'll see how Ms. Gustafson proceeds. Ms. Gustafson, you're aware of the objections against documents that are available. I think, at this point in time, if we are talking about documents, this will be about documents that are not available. So please proceed for the time being, and we'll see where we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 68, I'll repeat my last question to you. When you went to the MUP in Djakovica, did the MUP officials tell you how they had learned that it was these two Perforcis who had kidnapped your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Since there had been an attack on the SUP and the group was arrested, it must have been while they were giving a statement that they said that they had taken my husband, because they did not tell me the details of the story. They told me that it was brothers Perforci who had done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said, "it must have been while they were giving a statement." Did the MUP tell you whether they had statement -- a statement from these individuals or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: On that day, they only told me that it had been those persons who had kidnapped them. They told me that what with the statement they had given and -- or rather, in the statement they had given, after they were arrested, they apparently, so they told me, had told them that they had kidnapped them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify your last answer. Did the MUP officials tell you about a statement that they had received from these individuals, or did they just summarise what they had -- what had happened based on their general knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: They told me that those persons had kidnapped him, that they had handed him over to their commander by the name of Vuk, and that he had been taken over to Glodjane. I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, on this occasion, did the information you learned about what happened to your husband, did it just come from what the MUP told you had happened or did you see anything else that gave you further information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. I wasn't there at the scene. I only knew what they told me at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, there might be some confusion as far as the question is concerned. When you said, "I didn't see anything," Ms. Gustafson asked you whether you saw anything when you were at the MUP. Were you just told at that moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- about the arrest and what information they received, or did you see anything at that specific moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They only told me that they had arrested them - a group of them, in fact - and that they were among the group. The persons who had kidnapped him and who had handed him over to their commander by the name of Vuk, and that he was taken to Glodjane. I didn't see anything else apart from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said that what they told you was that these two individuals with the name of Perforci had handed your husband over to their commander by the name of Vuk and that he had been taken to Glodjane. Did they tell you on that occasion where he had been kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes, in the place called Dujak.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember anything else they told you on that occasion, any other details about what had happened to your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: No. No. In Djakovica, no, except that in this camp, if we can call it that, that Ramush Haradinaj was in charge of that. I didn't personally see him, nor do I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you say "this camp," what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: I meant Glodjane. I was told that that was where my husband had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at any later stage, after this visit to the Djakovica SUP, did you come to learn anything further about what had happened to your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes. In January, they called me from the MUP in Pec to tell me that the two brothers were in Pec in prison at Istok Dubrava. I asked how I could get hold of their statement to learn what had happened, because I had never in fact come to know what happened. The employee at the MUP there told me that they had stated that he had been killed and that he had -- was done for, but they didn't tell me any details. I know that in 1999 -- well, I'm not sure whether they were in fact sentenced, whether they were found guilty, but I know that in 1999 they were in prison in Dubrava. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said in January they called you from the MUP in Pec. Was that January of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when they called you from Pec, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: I went over to the SUP and I gave a statement again about when he had gone missing. Of course, before that, I had reported my husband going missing on the 16th of July, 1998. I wasn't able to do anything because I didn't know who or what they were. I -- nobody ever personally showed me these persons, to see who they were. I only knew that they were in prison in Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said that when they called you, in January, you asked if you could get hold of their statement. Did you ever get hold of their statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: No. No. I was only able to learn what they told me, but I never had it in my hand to be able to read what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you went to the SUP in January, did you learn anything else about what had happened to your husband, in addition to what you already knew from your visit to the Djakovica MUP in September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: No. No. I went, I attended every identification whenever I was called; but apart from that, no, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, your last question started with "and when you went to the SUP in January." I understood the previous question and answer to deal already with visiting the SUP in January, because your previous questions was: "And you said that when they called you, in January, you asked whether you could get hold of it," and then the witness said: "I didn't have anything in my hands at this moment." So the next question is a bit ignoring what the witness said before, and looks as if you are seeking different information; whereas, the question is about the same matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. She had said that she didn't get ahold of the statement, but I thought that she may have been given information in some other manner on that occasion. That was -- that was all I was asking after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you suggested that it was a different occasion, but perhaps I misunderstood your question. Perhaps you wanted to say: "And when you went to the SUP in January," that the emphasis is "when you went there," so subsequent to the previous answer but same occasion. I might have misunderstood it under those circumstances. I should not have asked you about it, but I was a bit confused; the witness apparently not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 68, I think there's a little confusion about what exactly happened in January when you went to the SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I think I was confused rather than anyone else in this courtroom. So I understood that when you went to the SUP, in January, you never had any statement in your hands and you did not receive any additional information, is that correctly understood, additional to what you knew already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In 1999, I didn't get anything or learn anything more than what I had previously known at Pec, save for the fact that he had been killed and that he had ended up in Lake Radonjic. I didn't learn anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was additional information, where he ended up. And that also included that he was killed, which is was not certain before. Yes. Thank you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, in 1999, you learned that your husband had been killed and that he ended up in Lake Radonjic. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber exactly how you learned this information. Who did you speak to? What did they tell you? What, if anything, did they show you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: At the identification, yes, but not at the SUP in Pec, except for the fact that they told me that he had been killed. In early September, everyone was able to identify their own dear and near by their pieces of clothing; whereas, I was unable to identify his remains because I didn't find any of his clothing there. Despite that, they still had their doubts and they still thought that his remains might be among the remains there. Perhaps it was down to me also. Perhaps I was in denial. I didn't want to accept that he may have been among them, and it was not until the year 2004, when his remains were in fact identified and when I was told that he was among them, that I accepted that at last.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness 68, I know this isn't very easy for you, but if you could please try to focus on what happened in January when you went to the SUP. And, on that occasion, you said you learned that your husband had been killed and that he had ended up in Lake Radonjic. In January, when you learned that information, please tell the Trial Chamber how you learned it. Who did you speak to? What did they tell you? And what, if anything, did they show you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: In January, save for the fact that they told me that the brothers stated that he had been killed and dumped at Lake Radonjic, I wasn't shown anything else and I wasn't told any other details. I went home and there was nothing else that I could do. I didn't know who to turn to. I had tried everything beforehand to find out more; but at the SUP, they did not tell me anything but what I told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 68. I just have one other question. It's just a minor matter that isn't 100 per cent clear from your statement. Your ethnicity is Serbian; and in your statement, you state that your husband was visiting some relatives who were Montenegrin, and I'd just like to ask you what exactly your husband's ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Yes. Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you, which is the following: Did you ever in your life ever see a document containing statements or a statement of one or the two brothers which you were told were involved in the disappearance of your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: A document, no, except for the fact that they told me in Djakovica that those were the ones who had kidnapped my husband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in your later conversations with the Office of the Prosecution, did you never see any document? Was never any document was shown to you where you were told that it could contain the statement or statements of the two persons mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: They read out a statement to me by Krist Perforci, or by his brother, I can't remember, where they stated that they had kidnapped my husband, that they had stopped him because he was in his own car. I really can't recall the details. It's been a long time. That's why I can't give you the exact details. That was the statement that they gave in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said, "they read out a statement." My question was about your conversations with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: I mean not that they didn't read it to me. They told me. It was -- I perhaps used a wrong term. They told me about him. They didn't read it to me, nor did I have the document in my hands to be able to read it. They conveyed what they had stated to them. They -- they conveyed that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understand your answer to refer to what happened at the time, whether in Djakovica or whether in Pec. Now, my question focused on your conversations with the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal, so more recently. Were you ever shown any statement in your conversations with the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Here or in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- either of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: During proofing, it was shown to me and I read it to refresh my memory. It's been a long time ago, and the names, of course, when I read them were familiar to me, because they remained etched in my memory; but before that occasion, I did not read the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that was the first time that you actually could look at a document containing the statement, a document which, if I understand you well, you had not seen before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/68
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Do the questions of the Chamber trigger any need for further questions? Then, Witness 68, this concludes your testimony. You've been in court only for a very limited time; but as you may have understood from the summary, the Chamber has received your statement and that is introduced into evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for answering questions, questions in relation to a matter, the disappearance of your husband, where it may have been very difficult for you to talk about it. Thank you very much, therefore, for coming and for answering questions. Madam Usher, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, we are in open session, although the curtains are down at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the curtains be drawn up again, perhaps with the assistance of some unauthorised officials of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I simply wanted to mention at this stage, in relation to the evidence that we've just heard, the Prosecution has disclosed certain documents about the prosecution of Leke Pervorfi, which do not reflect any conviction or sentence in respect of the alleged abduction, but merely in respect of the illegal possession of weapons. We will, in due course, seek to have that material reduced into the form of a stipulation for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These documents - I'm also looking at you, Ms. Gustafson - do they contain any information about what happened in court? I mean, a judgement is one thing. The transcript or any report of the proceedings, of course, is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There -- there's very limited information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very limited information.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It reflects dates, conviction, appeal against sentence, grounds of appeal against sentence, reduction of sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But what is apparent from the documents that there are is that he was not prosecuted, certainly not prosecuted to conviction in respect of any involvement and alleged abduction. Our understanding is that the other gentleman, Krist Perforci, who in fact is a cousin and not a brother, died in prison in a incident which is notorious and the subject of charges in other indictments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we'll look at that material. It's important, I think, that the Chamber receives, in order to be in a position to evaluate, the testimony of the witness and that the Chamber receives as much evidence as possible; and even then it might not -- it might not be easy to evaluate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because in some systems, even if someone confesses to a crime, sometimes that might not be sufficient to convict someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting anything about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- other than that you, the Trial Chamber, may have been left with the impression that those proceedings would have resulted in a conviction in respect of this matter, and that is an impression that needed to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not have raised the matter, I would have asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for further information in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate that the nature of the material it's best described as idiosyncratically presented, in the sense that different cases with different accused are woven into single documents, and it would be most straightforward, I suspect, for us to agree a stipulation which sets out the core information for the Trial Chamber, but perhaps Ms. Gustafson and I can discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're encouraged to enter into such discussions. Ms. Gustafson, I more or less interpret your body language at this moment that you're inclined to accept the invitation by Mr. Emmerson. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: On that topic, can I ask that we take the morning break now. There are a number of reasons for that. Firstly, there's the issue that was raised by Defence counsel this morning, and it would be nice to give Mr. Re a chance to organise himself to address those -- those issues. And, so for that -- for those reasons, if we could take the break now, I'm sure it would make the next witness's evidence a lot smoother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, before we invite the Prosecutor to call -- the Prosecution to call its next witness, an issue was raised not for the first time, as a matter of fact, because I think it was this week that I referred to a decision in May. I think I read paragraph 6 of that decision, which sets out the test for new exhibits not appearing on the 65 ter list, where I think we said that exhibits like pseudonym sheets, not matters of great substance, of course, that we would be flexible on that. Mr. Guy-Smith draws our attention to the fact that 25 exhibits on the Zivanovic exhibit list do not appear on the 65 ter list. It's a bit confusing that they receive 65 ter numbers. I do understand, let's take the neutral approach, that you use these numbers in order to get them uploaded in the system. At the same time, 65 ter, well, gives the impression that it refers to a 65 ter list, where they do not appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning to the Trial Chamber. With me this morning is Ms. Elena Martin Salgado, who has been assisting in preparation of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I note, of course, Mr. Guy-Smith's motion, which was just e-mailed to me a moment ago. We, of course, make an oral application and we move to add these documents to the 65 ter list. Whether it's a matter of substance is, of course, a matter of interpretation, and one would have to go to each document and argue, so to speak, the toss in relation to each one. Our general response is we move to add them to the list. Mr. Guy-Smith has pointed to no procedural or substantive prejudice in the documents being added to the list, to a virtual list. Your Honour is quite correct. With 65 ter numbers, it's the only way to get them into e-court and to have them appear in the proceedings, so to speak. In respect of all of the documents, the statement is dated, I think, it's the 7th, and we've disclosed the statement in August 2007, I think on the 20th of August, 2007. The Defence has had all of the documents since the latest the 24th of August, 2007. A large number -- a number of these documents we received this year in responses to requests for assistance. If I say annex 1, 2, 3, 48, 49, and 50, we received on the 15th of March after trial began from the Serbian authorities. It was posted to the Defence on the Electronic Disclosure Suite on the 10th of April. Annexes, 9, 11, 15, 16, 18, 25, 26, 28, 30, 32, and 86 were received on the 30th of March from the Serbian authorities and were placed on the EDS and disclosed to the Defence on the 10th of April, 2007. Annexes 52, 57, 58, 60, 62, 75, 81, 84 were actually received in October last year, and it appears -- I was trying to work out when they were disclosed. They were definitely disclosed by the very latest of August of this year. Annex 82, received on the 1st of March, 2007 [Realtime transcript read in error "1997"], was posted on the EDS on the 24th of July, 2007. Annex 56 was disclosed on the 10th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, annex 82, it was received on the 1st of March of --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this year? Yes, it reads "1997" on the transcript, but that should be "2007."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And annex 59 is the same document as annex -- as 65 ter 492, so that was already on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And there's one more, annex 88. We've had that since 1999. It's from the Milosevic investigation. So, in broad terms, there is no procedural or substantive prejudice to the Defence. They've had the documents for an -- a sufficient time to prepare their investigations. They've been on notice that we intended to use these particular military documents with this particular witness for some months now; most of the documents since January when we filed it, but the others since at least August. Most of the documents, the great majority, 95, 99 per cent, are just military documents, more military orders, combat reports, et cetera, and it is certainly in the interest of justice, in our submission, for the Trial Chamber to hear the evidence of what's in these documents as they're referred to in General Zivanovic's 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to -- to understand the military case, one must see these documents in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that on the 24th of August - is that what you said - is when the -- whether it should have been known by the Defence that these documents would be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the date on which we disclosed the -- the annexes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- in a bundle, and I think we gave them to the Trial Chamber within a week of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, on from that moment, you say they should be aware of that, but then let me just say, it's -- it's use of language, downplaying. Today it is the 11th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, to call the time period from the 24th of August until the 11th of October "some months" might be illustrative. It might be an illustration of downplaying what really happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the date when we gave them the annexes. We disclosed the statement on the -- the 15th of August, and the statement refers to each of those documents which were in the EDS, in which the Defence has had access to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That is a matter of months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is less than two months. You call that "some months," but the issue is that we are discussing in court this matter, where only a few days ago the Chamber made it perfectly clear that flexibility would be shown on minor matters; but, apart from that, as it appears in our decision of May, a proper application shall be made to add exhibits or to add documents to the 65 ter list, which, of course, has not been done. Now we are discussing these matters. It might be that the late -- that the time when these documents were received fully justify that. I'm not saying it does or it does not. But we're now spending time on it in court, where a proper application, if not earlier, at least then a couple of days ago, when the Chamber has specifically drawn the attention to this procedural requirement to the Prosecution. But apart from that, Mr. Guy-Smith, you would like to respond, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very briefly, because I don't want to take much court time. We filed a motion seeking clarification on the issue of Rule 65 ter procedure months ago, which is why this Chamber issued its decision. There is no following of the procedures that exist. We request that there be such a following of the procedures so that we can intelligently deal with the information that comes to us. The fact of something being put in the EDS system - and I'm not going to have an EDS conversation right now - is cold comfort at best. We receive thousands upon thousands upon thousands of pages of documents, which we have to plough through on the EDS system. There is decisional law all throughout this building with regard to whether or not that's adequate notice or not. The real issue here is an issue of adequate notice and justification for the admission of other substantive documents. The Prosecution does not seem wish to follow this rule. We request that they do so from now on, and we request that there be some form of sanction in the event that they don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we'll consider the matter. At the same time, the Chamber can't give a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- an answer right away, and I think I've sufficiently emphasized the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Part of what we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Part of what we're trying to do is we're trying to stop playing catchup, which is really what we've been doing in the last couple of months. It's that we're constantly playing catchup because we receive late disclosure, we receive late 92 ter statements, and we are in a position where we are scrambling in order to adequately deal with the Prosecution's case. We would like it to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I mean, it's the 20th of August. I mean, the 15th of August is late disclosure of this statement? The witness is testifying on the 11th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm speaking about a general difficulty that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not mix up matters. First of all, EDS disclosure and giving a list of annexes is, of course, not the same. We are not talking about thousands and thousands of documents in respect of this, so, therefore, it's not just EDS disclosure. Apart from that, the problems with providing 92 ter statements are a bit different from the problem we are dealing with at this moment; that is, adding documents to the 65 ter list. Let's not mix up everything. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't wish to mix up everything. It's only when we're doing an analysis of a 92 ter statement that rely on annexes, and we have to -- we have to, in fact, meld the two together to figure out what is an intelligent response so that we have objections for the Chamber to review them. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the objection is noted. At this point. I understand the Chamber is not in a position to deal with those specific annexes right now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- which I think points out what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I support that understanding. Mr. Re, are you ready to call Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly am, and I call retired Major-General Dragan Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: While he's coming in, can I just raise the issue of dealing with the annexes and the tab documents attached to his statement. There are some 90 documents which are annexed to his statement. I would propose, if it's acceptable to the Court, dealing with it in the same way we dealt with Mr. Stijovic's evidence; that is, allocating them numbering, having them marked for identification in sequence. Several of them have been -- several of them are already in evidence and are Defence exhibits. Of course, we'd skip those, because I'm obviously not going to take the witness to every document, and that way we'll keep them in the same order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will invite Mr. Registrar to assign numbers to them, which, of course, doesn't predict in any way what the Chamber will decide in terms of admission, so for purely administrative reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- may I just very briefly indicate, we've obviously tried to have some discussions in terms of timing. This is a witness whose cross-examination, I would anticipate, will take a little time, and I think we're all proceeding on the basis that there is no realistic prospect of him concluding his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was scheduled for two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I misunderstood. "Will take a little time" means much time. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The word "little" stayed on my mind and I had to reread it. Yes. "A little" is not the same "as little." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's also a 92 ter summary, if I could read that onto the record at the beginning. I didn't do that with Mr. Stijovic because there was -- the matter was unresolved when we walked into court. But as the Trial Chamber is aware, we resolved last night the issue of the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with some assistance of the Chamber, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you give evidence, you have to give a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Re, who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: First things first, your name is Dragan Zivanovic and you were born on the 8th of January, 1955 and you are a retired Major-General in the Army of the Republic of Serbia; before that, the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; and before that, the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you retired from the Army of Republic of Serbia on the 31st of March, 2006.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In front of you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And for the benefit of everyone here, the witness has a copy of his 92 ter statement and a copy of the annexes in a folder from 1 through to 90 in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: ... I want you to look at your statement, which is signed and dated the 9th of August, 2007. My first question to you is: Do you have the statement there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does it bear your signature and is it true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature and it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And if we were to ask you about the matters in that statement, would you give the same evidence as is contained in that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has agreed - of course, with the Chamber's assistance - with the Defence to delete the last sentence of paragraph 42, beginning with "we heard"; the entire paragraph of paragraph 47; the first sentence of paragraph 48, which begins with "I also"; and the words in line 5 of paragraph 94, in the English, "by the KLA." And with those redactions, which we will make at a later point, may it be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, are there any objections to admission of the 92 ter statement? Then, Mr. Registrar, I do not know - it's not yet uploaded - if the amended version is not yet uploaded, whether you can already assign a number to it. Yes. Then, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit Number P1017.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P1017 is then admitted into evidence. Decisions on annexes to follow after they have been tendered. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I'm going to ask you to elaborate on some of the matters which are in your statement, but first I'm going to read a summary of your statement onto the record so that the public can follow the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has a copy been given to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the booth has a copy. I'm sorry, I had it a moment ago. This is the summary of the statement, the Rule 92 statement, of Dragan Zivanovic: Dragan Zivanovic retired as a Major-General in the Army of the Republic of Serbia in 2006. He served in Kosovo with the VJ - that's Yugoslav Serbian army - from 1997 until its withdrawn in June 1999. He was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps' 125th Motorised Brigade from the 1st of September 1997 until the 12th of June, 1998, when he was appointed commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade. His area of responsibility included the municipalities of Pec, Decani, Istok, and Klina - I'm using the Serbian names because it's a Serbian witness - and the villages of Glodjane and Jablanica and the north-western tip of Lake Radonjic, including the Lake Radonjic canal area. The 125th Motorised Brigade increased in strength over 1998 from 1400 in January 1998 to 2.500. On the 28th of February, 1998, several policemen were killed in a military-style ambush on a MUP patrol in Likosane. The ambush demonstrated that the KLA was organising militarily. The MUP observed the KLA were training and building bunkers and trenches. Border crossings carrying arms from Albania into Kosovo and Metohija increased, and VJ border posts were reinforced to prevent these incursions. From 28th of February onwards, the 125th Motorised Brigade had standing orders for six hours combat readiness; but by May 1998, combat readiness had been reduced to one hour. As a direct result of KLA activity, the MUP set up check-points along the main roads. The KLA was unrelenting in attacking these check-points. After the Likosane attack of 28th of February, the Kosovska Mitrovica-Pec road was under the control of the KLA, and the 125th Motorised Brigade was forced to use the Kosovska Mitrovica- Pristina-Pec road instead. In 1997, a soldier could have travelled the whole of the Kosovska Mitrovica-Pec alone and unharmed. Combat groups were formed in the 125th Motorised Brigade in April 1998 to insist the MUP in maintaining the control of the Pec-Decani-Djakovica road. MUP units on this road were under constant KLA attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you please slow down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In April 1998, the KLA attacked VJ positions at the Lake Radonjic Filtration Plant. On 25th of April, Major-General Pavkovic ordered that "captured terrorists" be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and laws of war. The VJ had no presence in the area radiating eastward along the Pec-Decani-Djakovica road. The MUP entered the area occasionally, but it was controlled by the KLA. The chief of security of Zivanovic's brigade informed him that Ramush Haradinaj's headquarters were in the area of Glodjane. Zivanovic was informed that Haradinaj had between 500 to 1.000 armed trained men, trained for terrorist action. Zivanovic was also informed that Jablanica, a KLA stronghold, contained a prison where kidnapped Serbs, Roma, and loyal Albanians were kept. In May 1998, and as a result of the conflict with the KLA, the FRY Assembly passed a special law giving the VJ control of a five-kilometre strip of territory from the border. In May 1998, the VJ could no longer use the Pristina-Klina-Pec, Pristina-Klina-Djakovica, Kosovska Mitrovica-Pec, and Pec-Decani-Djakovica roads. The KLA realistically controlled the roads radiating eastwards towards Glodjane and all roads eastwards along the Pec-Djakovica road. The 125th was spared from the KLA attacks in the very early part of 1998. On 23rd of May, 1998, Zivanovic was taking 220 soldiers to the border along the Djakovica-Ponosevac-Morina road, when they were attacked by the KLA using mortars and hand-held rocket launchers. By mid-June 1998, his brigade was suffering three or four attacks per day. In late July/early August 1998, the 125th assisted the MUP in an operation to clear the Pec-Pristina road. In early August 1998, Combat Group 3 of the 125th assisted the MUP in the Dukagjini area to disarm KLA soldiers. It should say "an operation to disarm KLA soldiers." MUP patrols were being attacked daily by the KLA. MUP and 125th Brigade forces, numbering about 420, took Prilep after two days of resistance from the KLA, which had an estimated 60 soldiers. They then took Rznic. The MUP set up check-points which were attacked by the KLA, which then gained control. A large VJ-MUP combined operation took place against the KLA between 6th and 8th of September, 1998. The 125th Brigade units went as far as Zarki Pojas, and the MUP continued to Rznic and the Lake Radonjic canal area. Units from the 549th Motorised Brigade assisted MUP forces in taking Glodjane. That completes the summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what I'm going to do, Mr. Zivanovic, is I'm going to ask you about some questions about the things in the statement to elaborate and clarify some matters and show you -- refer you to some of the documents which are annexed to your statement. The first thing I want to ask you about is, in general terms, the border situation in early 1998, and in military terms, is significant of what was happening on the Albanian Kosovo state border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be unclear. You said "the first thing I want to ask you about." Is that an invitation to explain to us what the significance was?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The significance of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, but was it already a question? I noticed that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- might have been waiting for questions about these matters, or whether you invited him to answer this already as your first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's my first question, Mr. Zivanovic, to explain the significance of what was happening on the border in January, in early 1998.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the primary task of any member of the Army of Yugoslavia in Kosovo and Metohija, and thereby the 125th Motorised Brigade and border battalions, was to protect the state border. Under the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the border was guarded by the army; namely, the army guarded it in the 100-metre belt. Everything else was within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior; that is, the units in depth, the protection. In the beginning of 1998, the number of illegal crossings of the state border increased in the area of responsibility of the 125th Brigade, which was on the tripartite border of Montenegro, Serbia, and Albania, in the area of Morina. That was a stretch of 45 kilometres. Illegal crossings were particularly bad in the section between Morina village until the watchtower of Kosare, or in Albanian, Raqe Kosares [phoen]. The groups that crossed the border numbered from one person up to 200 persons, as was the case in April. The purpose of these illegal crossings was to go to the Republic of Albania, to purchase arms there, and to take those arms and military equipment into Kosovo and Metohija in order to arm the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just stop and ask you to pause there for a moment. Can Sanction be used for a moment. We wish to display paragraph 28 of your statement, in which you refer to the illegal bored crossings. Now, you're referring there, and you've just given an answer, about the illegal supply of weapons from Albania. Describe the magnitude of the problem as seen by the Yugoslav state officials of the transport of weapons across the Albanian border in early 1998.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a great problem for us for the following reasons: First, with the break-up of the armed forces of Albania, there resulted a situation in which the armed forces of Albania no longer guarded the weapons or the military equipment in their military depots, so it became accessible to civilians and potential smugglers of weapons. With the occurrence of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, there resulted a need for them to supply their own people with arms and to form the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army. That was the problem with illegal crossings for us, crossings from Kosovo and Metohija to Albania first, in order to purchase weapons. They purchased weapons by collecting funds at village level and region level, from donations from abroad, from their own diaspora, and donations from their own businessmen. They designated specific persons who were required to go across the border; plus, they had trained guides who knew the system of state border security very well, because they had monitored it for a couple of years back, and they were easily able to guide offenders across the border even in whole columns, whether they were going on foot or on mules, and take them back once they were loaded with cargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there any estimate of -- was there any estimate of how many weapons went across the border in the first three months of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the estimate of the Ministry of the Interior in the beginning of 1998, in Kosovo and Metohija, there was between 80.000 to 100.000 weapons. Official -- unofficial estimates went up to 200.000. At the end of 1998, after the voluntary surrender of a certain amount of weapons by certain villages, in September and October, we evaluated that there were about 400.000 weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about weapons coming across the border in the first few months of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of that year, in that section of 40 kilometres in my area, I reported that around 20.000 weapons had been carried across the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of weapons were -- was the VJ intercepting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were primarily weapons that later belonged to the army -- earlier belonged to the Army of Albania: Mainly Chinese-made weapons that were in the arsenal of the Army of Albania; semi-automatic rifles; automatic rifles of the Kalashnikov type; light machine guns; machine guns; hand-held launchers, two or three types of them with a range of 150 to 400 metres; 60-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars; and the accompanying equipment, clips, accessories, and ammunition for all types of weapons, beginning with the 7.62-millimetre round, 7.9, 12.5, 14.5, 12.7, 75-millimetres, 82-millimetres, and 120-millimetre shells for hand-held launchers, anti-personnel mines, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the heaviest weapons that were intercepted in that period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of April, the heaviest was the recoilless gun, 82-millimetre; mortars, 82-millimetres; a lot of ammunition for infantry weapons; recoilless guns; hand-held launchers; and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred a moment ago to columns going across the border, some on foot, some on mules, and going back once they were loaded with cargo. Can you describe in a little bit more detail these columns and how the goods were transported across the border. When I say "goods," I mean weapons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on our observation of the border belt and based on intelligence we received from state security, but primarily from observing done by border authorities, it was noticed that a convoy or a group that would go to purchase weapons and military equipment would gather at one point close to the border. It was usually close to a larger settlement called Tropoje. That's where the weapons and military equipment were brought on lorries, as far as we could see. They were distributed during the night or maybe sold from the lorries. I can't say which way it was done, because I wasn't there. And then, depending on their own estimates of how it was best to cross the border back, in one column or in groups of five or ten persons, they would go back. They mainly used areas that were not the choice routes of movement either for the passage of pedestrians or the cattle taken -- or rather, going across the border freely. They would choose routes where they thought there would be no patrols or no ambushes by the crew on the watchtower. I have to say that those 40 kilometres were secured by around 150 men on three to five watchtowers, depending on whether it was summertime or winter season. It is very difficult, indeed, to cover 40 kilometres with one shift of men consisting of 30/40 men. So the place of the ambushes changed, but they had obviously been very well prepared, because they had observed the positioning of our border authorities and they would use the gaps to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the crossings typically by day or by night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the crossings took place by night or in the early morning hours; exceptionally, also during the day when the weather was bad, when there was fog, rain spells, blustery weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the crossing points used to get across the border?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean legal crossings, there were no legal crossings. As for the illegal crossings, there were -- they would cross along all the directions. They would cross even Bogicevica Mount, which was more than 2500 metres above sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did the weapons go to once they crossed from Albania into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They would go to the staffs existing at village levels. These staffs would then decide, depending on when the teams of people were sent, to whom the weapons would be delivered to. They distributed the weapons to volunteers who wanted to join the ranks of terrorists. Later on, it was done through mandatory mobilisation, to use the military term of "mobilisation," but what they did was to compel the population, mostly the young ones, to take weapons and to become members of terrorist groups and armed formations, which in their mind had specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you describe the border posts which are in paragraph 28, you say: "The border posts were reinforced to try to prevent these incursions." Can you describe to the Trial Chamber what a border post comprised of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take the example of the Morina border post. It's at the saddle of Morina, the village of Ponosevac, and the villages of Gornja and Donja Morina, Tropolja. The area of responsibility of this border post is 13 kilometres wide from Boka or Kamen. Across the village of Prevoj, you reach the border post of Kosare. It had between 30 to 40 men, including the commander and the deputy who were professional officers. Now, how did they provide for the security? The very watchtower, the border post was some 20 metres from the border as the crow flies. There existed a plan which changed daily based on the decision of the commander of the company or the commander of the battalion stationed in Djakovica. A certain number of patrols, let's take an example: On a given day, two patrols would be organised and two ambushes. The patrols would normally comprise three, five, or eight men. At times, if information was received about certain problems detected, then the strengths of the patrols would increase. The patrols would be sent at different times to different directions, but predominantly within that 100-metre border belt. The patrols would be moving overtly, because they were in their own territory securing their own country. Exceptionally, as late -- as problems emerged and as terrorists started attacking border authorities occasionally, the patrols would be moving through their territory or through open spaces covertly. They would either skirt, as such, clearings or scurry through them. As for ambushes, they were also set at specific times. There would be two- to three-hour ambushes and, exceptionally, six-hour ambushes that were set along an axis where it was expected that offenders might appear, attempting to cross the border illegally. This could be in both ways or only in one way. Ambushes would be set on such locations at a specific time. They had to maintain the regime of discipline and keep quiet and unnoticeable. If they do manage to maintain that regime, then they remained undetected and were able to do their job; otherwise, they would be noticed by the offenders trying to cross the border illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just referred to ambushes and patrols. What was the frequency of the ambushes and patrols in the first four months of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: By -- or rather, until the month of April, the situation was practically as per normal, and two ambushes could be set on a 24-hour basis, and this was, of course, quite a burden for the men. From the month of April, with the increased number of illegal crossings, the Pristina Corps stepped up certain border posts and replenished them with additional men, particularly those charged with reconnaissance in order to timely detect any problems. Even these reinforcements could not go on for long. If you had some 30 to 40 men who were at the border post and if they were further reinforced with 20 men, this meant that their strengths could go up by 50 per cent. The reinforcements were not charged with patrolling the areas; rather, they were charged mostly with reconnoitering and observing from the watchtowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clarify your answer where you said "the situation was practically as per normal and two ambushes could be set up on a 24-hour basis." What was normal about two ambushes in a 24-hour basis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is only normal for one to take place at night and the other one by day. The people had to be engaged because that was the tactics of the border service according to the rules governing the border service. There could be no slacking along the border belt. The discipline had to be maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that on a quiet day there were two ambushes set upper day but on a busy day there were more, or are you saying something else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying precisely that. On a quiet day, there were two ambushes, and the two ambushes could not take place at the same time. One had to take place during the night and the other one during the day. If we had one ambush during the day that was supposed to be on duty for two hours, the remaining ten hours would pass by without any ambushes in that particular area of a given border post. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying. And if we don't have a patrol, then this area of 13 kilometres would only be observed as much as could be observed from a watchtower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A few moments ago you talked about reinforcing -- orders for reinforcement. In paragraph 28, you refer to a particular order of General Pavkovic on the 18th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's at tab 3 or annex 3, if that could be displayed in e-court, please, and the number of it read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, have you already assigned numbers to the list?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's 65 ter number 01930, and it will be marked for identification as P1021.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have the -- Mr. Zivanovic, do you have tab 3 open in front of you? Could you go to the document at tab 3 there. It's an order of the 18th of March, 1998 signed by General Pavkovic, Major-General Pavkovic, commander of the Pristina Corps, headed: "Increased DG - that's sabotage group - and Order." It says: "Due to the worsening security situation in the corps zones of responsibility and the border area, in order to prevent violation of the border regime in the Pristina Corps zone of responsibility, I issue the following order," and he orders an increase in security. Was that one of the types of orders that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. This is an order relating to the subordinate units of the corps command, asking them to send reinforcements to certain areas to assist border battalions and border posts. Specifically, this order provides for the following: That out of the 125th Motorised Brigade, 20 men were to be deployed to the Kosare border post and re-subordinated to the border post commander for providing further border security. These men were sent out of the Pec garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is the significance of that particular order, in relation to the incursions and the security situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The significance lies in the following: We felt the need to try and prevent, as the Army of Yugoslavia, these illegal crossings and to prevent arms trafficking ending up in the terrorists being armed. By "the terrorists," I mean the so-called KLA, which caused a great problem for us. The corps command had the authority to do this because these border battalions and our brigades were subordinated to him. By sending these reinforcements, he tried to step up border security and prevent illegal crossings. If border -- illegal border crossings could not be prevented, at least attempts should be made to seize the cargo, the weapons being smuggled at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just used the word "terrorists," and said "I mean the so-called KLA." If you can go to paragraph 21 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we just display that in Sanction for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: ... in your statement, you said: "The VJ documents I refer to in this statement refer to 'terrorists,' 'terrorist and sabotage groups (DTG),' and terrorist and sabotage forces (DTS),' These terms were used to refer primarily to the Kosovo Liberation Army." That's in your statement. I wish to refer you also to MFI P955 [Realtime transcript read in error "P9555"], which is an order -- sorry, it's some information from the Deputy Federal Minister of Yugoslavia, dated the 16th of March, 1998. You won't find it in your bundle, but it will come up on the screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you said P955?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, yes, that's clear now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to explain why the word "terrorist" or "DTG" or "DTS" was used in many of the communications at that time rather than "KLA" or "UCK."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the official documents we received from the highest levels of the VJ, they used this terminology; and, in reality, that is what was the case. A terrorist group could have between three to five, ten, fifteen, or twenty men. Why was it referred to as "the sabotage terrorist group"? Well, I believe this is the same worldwide, that this is a group attacking the official bodies, the official authorities, and endangers the persons and properties both of individuals and the institutions of a country. If there were several sabotage and terrorist groups, we referred to them as "sabotage and terrorist forces." The term "KLA" was always written in inverted commas. It meant the Kosovo Liberation Army. Why did we put it into inverted commas? Because we did not wish to recognise that force, since in the country there was one regular army and that was the Yugoslavia Army; that is, the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Had we accepted and recognised the term "Kosovo Liberation Army," it would have meant that we accepted them as the enemy but as our partner. There were tendencies that went several years back to establish the Kosovo Liberation Army with the final goal of accelerating the secession of Kosovo and Metohija and the proclamation of their independence from the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's why this term was very important to us. Besides, we didn't have the information to the effect who was in charge on the other side and who could be the person to negotiate with, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you can look on the screen in front of you, there's the document I referred to a moment ago, which is the information from March 1998 from the Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, maybe if it could be scrolled down or the next page could be shown, and the next one if that could be made bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zivanovic, do you recall seeing this particular document as of the date of its dissemination, that's in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not in a position to see this before. This is the first -- the first time I see this. At that time, I was the Chief of Staff of the 125th Motorised Brigade stationed in Kosovska Mitrovica; whereas, this is the level of the Foreign Ministry, which was far above my head --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: The witness said "Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I make -- I can comment now that you've asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question is simply this: Whether what you see there, and where it says, "We believe that the operations by organs of the MUP cannot be described as an internal armed conflict, in the sense of Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and the Law on of Armed Conflict. "This concerns a police action of preventing crimes, acts of terrorism.
